name: authentication-enforcer
intent: Put one request-boundary checkpoint in front of protected actions that decides whether authentication is required, delegates credential verification to a replaceable mechanism, and attaches the resulting subject to request-scoped context before dispatch, so coverage is uniform without making handlers understand credentials.
problem: When each handler decides whether and how to authenticate, protection is duplicated or omitted on exceptional paths, credential formats and user stores leak into business code, and a mechanism or policy change requires editing every handler instead of one auditable boundary.
context: Server-side request processing — web APIs, web applications and service endpoints — where many handlers share one protection policy, credentials arrive through a uniform convention (Authorization header, cookie, session id), verification technology must be replaceable or differ per route, and the runtime provides a request-pipeline hook (servlet filter, middleware chain, framework guard). Applies to session-based and token-based authentication alike; permissions and roles are out of scope. Three implementation strategies exist: (1) Container-Managed Authentication — the runtime container owns the checkpoint and realm configuration; (2) Authentication Provider Strategy — a custom provider behind a narrow interface, swapped without touching handlers; (3) JAAS Login Module Strategy — pluggable via standard JAAS configuration, supporting multifactor authentication via smart cards, biometrics, or third-party IdPs. The pattern is equally applicable at the edge level (API gateway, ingress proxy) and the service level (in-process middleware).
benefits: Protection is defined once: every route behind the checkpoint gets identical enforcement, and a new handler cannot silently omit its authentication check under a default-deny policy.
The verification mechanism is replaceable — password store, LDAP, OAuth2/OIDC token, mutual TLS, SSO/SAML — without touching handlers, which depend only on the verified subject.
Failure behaviour is uniform and auditable: one place issues the challenge (401 with WWW-Authenticate, login redirect) and one place logs rejected attempts.
The policy of which resources require authentication becomes reviewable configuration (path map, route wrapper, guard binding) instead of logic scattered through handlers.
Handlers and the authorization layer receive a ready principal, so identity concerns disappear from business code.

Supports Zero Trust architectures: every request is authenticated regardless of network position, and the checkpoint can enforce additional signals (device posture, tenant context) before attaching a subject.
Consolidating authentication into one enforcement point reduces the attack surface compared to scattered credential checks and makes coverage auditing tractable (OWASP ASVS V4.0 §V1.4.1).
tradeoffs: The central allow-list is a single point of failure: one wrong public-path entry exposes an endpoint, one wrong protected entry locks users out — the risk moves from scattered code into one high-stakes configuration.
The checkpoint is framework-shaped (servlet filter, middleware function, guard class); enforcement code does not port between stacks and is rewritten when the framework changes.
Debugging spans three places — the enforcer, the delegated mechanism and any gateway in front — and a 401 may be produced before application code ever runs.
Non-HTTP entry points (scheduled jobs, message consumers, internal service calls) never traverse the pipeline, so the checkpoint can create a false sense of complete coverage.
Challenge (401) and forbid (403) semantics belong to the delegated mechanism and are easy to conflate with the authorization layer, producing misleading responses.
Per-request overhead is determined by the mechanism — token introspection or a central session lookup — so scalability is bounded by that store, not by the interception itself.

At the edge level (API gateway), the enforcer becomes a critical infrastructure dependency; its misconfiguration or compromise affects every service behind it. Defense in depth — service-level verification in addition to edge verification — is required for high-assurance systems (NIST SP 800-207).

participants.responsibility: The pipeline checkpoint: decides whether the target resource requires authentication, extracts credentials through the shared transport convention, invokes the mechanism and either attaches the verified subject to the request or issues the challenge.

The delegated, replaceable component that verifies the presented credentials against a user store or token issuer and returns a subject; the enforcer never knows how verification works. Three strategies: container-managed (runtime realm), custom provider (pluggable interface), or JAAS login module.
The convention by which credentials reach the enforcer (Authorization header, cookie, session identifier, client certificate) — a contract shared with the mechanism.
The verified identity produced by the mechanism and attached to the request context.
Request-scoped carrier that makes the subject available to handlers and the authorization layer without re-verification.
The endpoint whose business logic assumes an authenticated caller and never authenticates itself.
The uniform failure behaviour for unauthenticated requests: 401 with a challenge header, redirect to login, or mechanism-specific negotiation.
Declarative configuration (path prefix map, route wrapper, guard binding) that records which routes are public and which require authentication. Changes independently of the mechanism.

use_cases: Web APIs where every route except health and login requires a bearer token, and the checkpoint is mounted in front of the whole router.
Multi-tenant applications with mixed protection levels: public marketing pages, session-protected tenant UI and token-protected integration endpoints behind one enforcement layer.
Services that must accept several credential types at once — browser sessions, mobile JWTs, mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic — while keeping one uniform enforcement point.
Credential-technology migration (basic auth to OIDC, on-premises LDAP to SSO) where enforcement stays put while the mechanism behind it is swapped.
Regulated environments where every rejected authentication attempt has to be logged centrally and identically across all endpoints.
Legacy applications with authentication checks scattered through servlets or handlers that must be consolidated behind one intercepting layer before an audit.

Zero Trust microservices where every internal service verifies JWTs independently (per-service verification) while an ingress gateway provides the first checkpoint — the enforcer exists at both layers.
OIDC/OAuth2 migration where an existing session-based app adds bearer-token support; the mechanism adapts to both while the enforcement point remains unchanged.
Multi-tenant SaaS platforms where tenant isolation depends on the enforcer resolving a tenant identifier from the token before the handler processes any data.

Platform-as-a-Service with mounted sub-applications where a parent ASGI middleware dispatches per-path authentication requirements from a config registry, injecting identity into ASGI scope for all sub-apps.

Spring Security servlet applications that use a SecurityFilterChain with anyRequest().authenticated() and an AuthenticationManager/AuthenticationProvider chain, so controllers consume the SecurityContext rather than parse credentials.
ASP.NET Core APIs that register JWT or cookie schemes, call UseAuthentication before dependent middleware, and use a fallback authorization policy to make authenticated access the default.

An nginx ingress location using auth_request to delegate identity verification to a central authentication service, forwarding only after a 2xx result and propagating 401/403 failures while services still verify their own trust boundary.
avoid_when: A single-purpose script or one-endpoint application: an inline check is simpler and the boundary indirection buys nothing.

A trusted upstream has already authenticated the request and cryptographically binds the identity (for example, service-mesh mTLS): consume a verified subject descriptor after validating the trust boundary instead of blindly re-authenticating or trusting forwarded headers.

Identity is already established and only permissions are missing: use the authorization-enforcer, which decides whether this subject may perform the requested action; this pattern only establishes identity.

An MVC Secure Base Action already owns the sole front-controller security lifecycle: extend that entry point rather than adding a second checkpoint, while keeping credential verification delegated and separately testable.
Every action needs a distinct step-up or re-authentication flow: an explicit action-level flow can express the transaction better, although a baseline enforcer may still protect the route.

The application has non-HTTP entry points that never traverse this pipeline (jobs, consumers, internal calls): add an equivalent checkpoint or document the separate trust model instead of claiming complete mediation.

A pure static frontend has no server-side resource to protect: do not remove enforcement from the backend/API merely because browser sign-in is delegated to an IdP; the service that owns data still needs an authentication boundary.
anti_patterns: Verification logic inside the enforcer: the checkpoint also owns the user store, password hashes or token parsing, so the mechanism cannot be swapped and the boundary cannot be tested without real credentials; keep verification in an Authenticator.
Fail-open policy map: unmatched routes are treated as public, so a newly added endpoint is exposed without a security review; default to protected and list only deliberate public exceptions.

Using the checkpoint as authorization: it returns 403 for a subject lacking permission, blurring authentication failure with access denial and making policy ownership unclear; let the authorization-enforcer make the 403 decision after identity is established.
Assuming the enforcer covers every surface while message consumers, schedulers and internal calls enter the system without traversing the pipeline.
Hardcoded fallback permissions that override explicit denials — a privilege-escalation vector that is invisible to integration tests.
Trusting forwarded identity headers from the client without stripping and replacing them from the auth result — clients can inject spoofed identity claims.
Global middleware applied to health checks and public endpoints causing false-positive 401/403 responses and degraded observability.
Re-verifying the subject inside the handler after the enforcer has already verified it — duplicates identity logic and risks inconsistent results.
Storing tokens or credentials in browser localStorage for SPAs instead of HTTP-only cookies or in-memory handling — enables XSS-based token theft.
design_principles: Single responsibility: the enforcer decides whether authentication is required; the mechanism decides how it succeeds.
Separation of concerns: authentication (identity) is kept apart from authorization (permission).
Information hiding: handlers depend only on the verified subject, never on credentials or the verification mechanism.
Fail-safe defaults: requests that match no explicit public rule are treated as protected.
Open/closed: new mechanisms are registered with the checkpoint, not edited into it.
Complete mediation: every request must pass through the checkpoint — no shortcut or bypass is permitted.
Fail-closed: deny on any uncertainty — malformed credentials, timeout, network partition, unknown route — never pass a request through when the checkpoint cannot establish identity.
Zero Trust: the checkpoint authenticates every request regardless of network origin; internal network position grants no implicit trust.
Defense in depth: edge-level enforcement is complemented by service-level verification; the two layers are independent and do not assume the other is correct.
Auditability: all authentication outcomes (success and failure) are logged in one place with the reason, timestamp, principal, and source IP — never credentials or tokens.
best_practices: Default deny: require authentication unless a route is explicitly declared public, and review the public surface like code.
Keep verification in the mechanism; the enforcer only transports credentials, delegates the check and attaches the subject.
Issue the challenge in exactly one place with correct semantics (401 plus WWW-Authenticate; 403 belongs to authorization).
Attach the verified subject to a request-scoped security context; never leave it in globals, statics or thread-locals that outlive the request.
Log rejected attempts and mechanism failures centrally, and never log credentials or tokens.
Cover non-HTTP entry points explicitly — either route them through an equivalent checkpoint or document the different trust model.
Test denial behaviour as part of release gating: confirm that invalid, expired, and missing tokens return 401 and never reach route execution.
Pair centralized enforcement with coverage testing: enumerate every protected route and verify it uses the shared control path; a partial implementation leaves unguarded routes (OWASP A01 / CWE-284).
Align session expiry, token revocation, and access reviews so the enforcement decision reflects current identity state rather than stale entitlements.

Use defense in depth: configure the edge-level checkpoint (gateway) for coarse validation and rate limiting; use service-level enforcement for fine-grained identity context. Never assume the outer checkpoint is sufficient.
Normalize paths before auth checks to prevent bypass via path variation (trailing slashes, encoded segments).

For ASGI/FastAPI platforms: inject identity via scope['state'] rather than headers for intra-process communication; strip client-provided identity headers and replace with values derived from the verified token.

When using OIDC/OAuth2: validate all token claims server-side (signature, issuer, audience, expiry, nonce) before trusting them; client-side validation alone is insufficient (RFC 8725 JWT Best Practices).
Cache verification material (public keys, issuer metadata) with TTL-bound expiration; never cache verified subjects across requests without explicit re-verification on expiry.
Align with NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust) and OWASP ASVS V4.0 §V1.4.1: verify every access path, not just the majority of routes.

https://designingsecuresoftware.com/text/ch4-enforce-patterns — Complete Mediation pattern: all access paths must go through the same security check, implemented as a single gate or functionally identical code across multiple gates.

https://auditbuffet.com/patterns/ab-002248 — AuditBuffet: centralized auth middleware; one-file enforcement surface; CWE-284 and OWASP A01 coverage criteria; Next.js middleware.ts for edge-level protection.

Lampson, Abadi, Burrows & Wobber, 'Authentication in Distributed Systems' (1992) — foundational reference monitor concept; authentication vs authorization distinction; channel-based principal authentication.

Fernandez, Sinibaldi, 'More Patterns for Operating System Access Control' (EuroPLoP 2003) — Authenticator pattern as single point to receive and verify subject identity; Reference Monitor as intercepting enforcement mechanism.
NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture; no implicit trust based on network location; continuous verification principle.
NIST SP 800-162 — Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC); policy management vs enforcement separation; AC-3 access enforcement requirements.

https://guides.rubyonrails.org/security.html — Rails authentication generator, has_secure_password, authenticate_by and session-backed authentication guidance.

related_patterns_notes.authenticator: The Authenticator is the delegated verifier, not the boundary policy: it checks credential evidence and returns a subject, while the Authentication Enforcer decides route coverage, invokes it and issues the challenge; direction: downstream
related_patterns_notes.authorization-enforcer: Authentication enforcer runs upstream; the authorization enforcer receives the verified subject produced by authentication and makes access-control decisions. The two are distinct responsibilities and should not be conflated in a single component; direction: upstream
related_patterns_notes.security-context: The security context is the request-scoped carrier created by the authentication enforcer to hold the verified subject for downstream use by handlers and authorization; direction: produced-by
related_patterns_notes.secure-base-action: In MVC frameworks the Secure Base Action consolidates security operations (auth, authz, audit) into a single front-controller; the authentication enforcer is the auth portion of that consolidation; direction: component-of
related_patterns_notes.intercepting-validator: Both patterns interpose on a request pipeline; the intercepting-validator handles data validation while the authentication enforcer handles credential validation and identity establishment; direction: parallel
related_patterns_notes.complete-mediation: Complete-mediation (Saltzer & Schroeder) is the principle that all accesses must go through the checkpoint; the authentication enforcer is the concrete application of that principle for identity; direction: embodies
related_patterns_notes.reference-monitor: The authentication enforcer is a reference monitor for authentication decisions: it intercepts every request, validates credentials, and either allows the request to proceed with a subject or blocks it with a challenge. Complete mediation, tamperproof, and assurance (small/simple code) are the three requirements it should satisfy; direction: embodies
related_patterns_notes.subject-descriptor: The subject attached to the security context by the enforcer is described by the Subject Descriptor pattern; the descriptor encodes what the handler can safely use about the identity; direction: produces
related_patterns_notes.gatekeeper: Gatekeeper is the edge-level specialization: a dedicated validation and security boundary at the system perimeter that handles authentication, rate limiting, and input sanitization before requests reach internal services; direction: specializes
related_patterns_notes.edge-level-authentication: Authentication at the system boundary by a shared component (API gateway, ingress proxy) — the architectural placement of the authentication enforcer in a microservices or Zero Trust topology; direction: same-pattern
related_patterns_notes.service-level-authentication: Authentication inside each service (shared library or sidecar) — complementary to edge-level; defense in depth requires both. Authentication enforcer can be deployed at either layer or both; direction: same-pattern
